steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our NLP paper introducing Prometheus, an open-source language model trained to do fine-grained evaluation of generated text with custom score rubrics. Motivate it from the problems of human evaluation, conventional metrics and proprietary LLM evaluators, introduce the new feedback dataset and the model, summarize the main results, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Evaluating machine-generated text: human evaluation vs automated metrics
- LLMs (GPT-4) as evaluators and their disadvantages (closed-source, versioning, cost)
- Limitation of current resources: generic, coarse-grained rubrics
- Our proposal: Prometheus + the Feedback Collection
- Main results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Evaluating machine-generated text
  - long-standing NLP challenge; essential in LLM era to understand properties/behaviors (cite)
  - human evaluation predominant: reliable, nuanced/subjective dimensions
  - humans discern important factors: brevity, creativity, tone, cultural sensitivities
  - BLEU, ROUGE etc. miss depth/granularity of human eval (cite)
- LLMs as evaluators
  - GPT-4 as evaluator, potential parity with human eval (cite)
  - aptly prompted -> emulate fineness of human evaluations
  - disadvantages of proprietary LLMs:
    - 1. Closed-source Nature: transparency, internal workings not disclosed; hinders academic efforts to refine; fair evaluation under for-profit control, neutrality/autonomy
    - 2. Uncontrolled Versioning: version updates beyond users' control (cite); reproducibility; undermines findings tied to versions, esp. evaluation
    - 3. Prohibitive Costs: four LLM variants x four sizes (7B to 65B), GPT-4, 1000 instances -> over $2000; bad for limited budgets
- Limitation of current resources
  - GPT-4 can score with customized rubrics
  - current resources: generic single-dimensional metrics, too domain/task-specific (EM, Rouge) or coarse-grained (helpfulness/harmlessness) (cite); left side of Figure 1
  - AlpacaFarm (cite) prompt: single definition of preference, generally preferred response
  - preferences vary by application and values
  - users want custom rubric: “Which LLM generates responses that are playful and humorous”, “Which LLM answers with particularly care for cultural sensitivities?”
  - initial experiments: largest open-source LLM (70B) insufficient vs proprietary

  - Prometheus, 13B LM; fine-grained evaluation like GPT-4; open-source, reproducible, inexpensive
  - Feedback Collection: diverse fine-grained user score rubrics, realistic demands (Figure 2); thousands of unique preference criteria via user-injected rubric
  - vs prior feedback datasets (cite): custom not generic rubrics -> generalize to practical, diverse preferences
  - first to explore reference materials, esp. ‘Reference Answers’

  - fine-tune Llama-2-Chat-13B
  - 45 rubrics, three test sets (MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, Feedback Bench): Pearson 0.897 with humans; GPT-4 0.882; GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.392

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Evaluating the quality of machine-generated text has been a challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for a long time, and it is especially essential now in the era of Large Language Models (LLMs), to understand their properties and behaviors. Human evaluation has always been the main method, because it is reliable and can assess nuanced and subjective dimensions in texts. In many situations humans can naturally tell what the most important factors of assessment are, like brevity, creativity, tone, and cultural sensitivities. On the other hand, conventional automated evaluation metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE) can't capture the depth and granularity of human evaluation.

Using LLMs (e.g. GPT-4) as an evaluator has gotten a lot of attention because it could be on par with human evaluation. Initial investigations and observations show that LLMs can emulate the fineness of human evaluations when they are prompted well. But while the merits of using proprietary LLMs for evaluation are clear, there are some critical disadvantages:

- 1. Closed-source Nature: Because LLMs are proprietary, there are transparency concerns, since the internal workings are not disclosed to the broader academic community. This lack of transparency gets in the way of collective academic efforts to refine or improve their evaluation capabilities. It also puts fair evaluation, which is a core tenet in academia, under control of a for-profit entity, and raises concerns about neutrality and autonomy.

- 2. Uncontrolled Versioning: Proprietary models get version updates that are often beyond the users' purview or control. This makes reproducibility a challenge. Reproducibility is a cornerstone of scientific inquiry, so any inconsistency from version changes can undermine the robustness of research findings that depend on specific versions of the model, especially for evaluation.

- 3. Prohibitive Costs: The financial constraints of LLM APIs are not trivial. For example, evaluating four LLMs variants across four sizes (from 7B to 65B) with GPT-4 on 1000 evaluation instances can cost over $2000. These scaling costs can be prohibitive, especially for academic institutions or researchers with limited budgets.

- Limitation of current resources: GPT-4 can use custom rubrics; current resources generic/single-dimensional (EM, Rouge / helpfulness/harmlessness), Figure 1 left; AlpacaFarm single preference definition; preferences vary; example custom rubrics (playful and humorous; cultural sensitivities); largest open-source LLM (70B) insufficient
- Proposal: Prometheus, 13B, open-source, reproducible, inexpensive; Feedback Collection (Figure 2), thousands of preference criteria, custom not generic rubrics; first to explore ‘Reference Answers’
- Results: Llama-2-Chat-13B; 45 rubrics, 3 test sets, Pearson 0.897 vs GPT-4 0.882, GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.392; pairwise 58.67% over GPT-4, 79.57% vs GPT-3.5-Turbo; 1222 rubrics, 4 test sets; 2 unseen human preference datasets, beats two reward models
- Contributions: Feedback Collection; Prometheus; experiments on reference materials + feedback fine-tuning

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Evaluating the quality of machine-generated text has been a challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for a long time, and it is especially essential now in the era of Large Language Models (LLMs), to understand their properties and behaviors. Human evaluation has always been the main method, because it is reliable and can assess nuanced and subjective dimensions in texts. In many situations humans can naturally tell what the most important factors of assessment are, like brevity, creativity, tone, and cultural sensitivities. On the other hand, conventional automated evaluation metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE) can't capture the depth and granularity of human evaluation.

Using LLMs (e.g. GPT-4) as an evaluator has gotten a lot of attention because it could be on par with human evaluation. Initial investigations and observations show that LLMs can emulate the fineness of human evaluations when they are prompted well. But while the merits of using proprietary LLMs for evaluation are clear, there are some critical disadvantages:

- 1. Closed-source Nature: Because LLMs are proprietary, there are transparency concerns, since the internal workings are not disclosed to the broader academic community. This lack of transparency gets in the way of collective academic efforts to refine or improve their evaluation capabilities. It also puts fair evaluation, which is a core tenet in academia, under control of a for-profit entity, and raises concerns about neutrality and autonomy.

- 2. Uncontrolled Versioning: Proprietary models get version updates that are often beyond the users' purview or control. This makes reproducibility a challenge. Reproducibility is a cornerstone of scientific inquiry, so any inconsistency from version changes can undermine the robustness of research findings that depend on specific versions of the model, especially for evaluation.

- 3. Prohibitive Costs: The financial constraints of LLM APIs are not trivial. For example, evaluating four LLMs variants across four sizes (from 7B to 65B) with GPT-4 on 1000 evaluation instances can cost over $2000. These scaling costs can be prohibitive, especially for academic institutions or researchers with limited budgets.

Despite these limitations, proprietary LLMs like GPT-4 are able to evaluate scores based on customized score rubrics. Current resources, specifically, are limited to generic, single-dimensional evaluation metrics, which are either too domain/task-specific (e.g. EM, Rouge) or coarse-grained (e.g. helpfulness/harmlessness), as shown in the left side of Figure 1. For instance, the prompt of AlpacaFarm gives a single definition of preference, and asks the model to pick the model response that is generally preferred. But response preferences vary depending on specific applications and values. In real-world scenarios, users may be interested in a customized rubric like “Which LLM generates responses that are playful and humorous” or “Which LLM answers with particularly care for cultural sensitivities?” Yet in our initial experiments we see that even the largest open-source LLM (70B) is not enough to evaluate based on a customized score rubric, compared to proprietary LLMs.

So we propose Prometheus, a 13B LM that aims to induce the fine-grained evaluation capability of GPT-4, while being open-source, reproducible, and inexpensive. First we create the Feedback Collection, a new dataset that is made to capture diverse and fine-grained user assessment score rubrics that represent realistic user demands (an example is in Figure 2). We design the Feedback Collection with this in mind, and it has thousands of unique preference criteria encoded by a user-injected score rubric. Unlike prior feedback datasets, it uses custom and not generic preference score rubrics, to train models to flexibly generalize to practical and diverse evaluation preferences. Also, as far as we know, we are the first to explore how important it is to include various reference materials, in particular the ‘Reference Answers’, to effectively induce fine-grained evaluation capability.

We fine-tune Llama-2-Chat-13B on the Feedback Collection to create Prometheus. On 45 customized score rubrics sampled across three test sets (MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, Feedback Bench), Prometheus gets a Pearson correlation of 0.897 with human evaluators, which is similar to GPT-4 (0.882) and a lot better than GPT-3.5-Turbo (0.392). Unexpectedly, when human evaluators are asked to choose the feedback with better quality in a pairwise setting, Prometheus was preferred over GPT-4 58.67% of the time, and it greatly outperformed GPT-3.5-Turbo with a 79.57% win rate. Also, when we measure the Pearson correlation with GPT-4 evaluation across 1222 customized score rubrics across 4 test sets (MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, Feedback Bench, Flask Eval), Prometheus has higher correlation than GPT-3.5-Turbo and Llama-2-Chat 70B. Finally, when testing on 2 unseen human preference datasets (MT Bench Human Judgments, HHH Alignment), Prometheus outperforms two state-of-the-art reward models and GPT-3.5-Turbo, which shows its potential as a universal reward model.

Our contributions are:

- • We introduce the Feedback Collection dataset, designed specifically to train an evaluator LM. Compared to previous feedback datasets, it has customized scoring rubrics and reference answers in addition to the instructions, responses, and feedback.

- • We train Prometheus, the first open-source LLM specialized for fine-grained evaluation, which can generalize to diverse, real-world scoring rubrics beyond a single-dimensional preference like helpfulness and harmlessness.

- • We run extensive experiments that show that we can induce evaluation capability into language models by appending reference materials (reference answers, fine-grained score rubrics) and fine-tuning on feedback. Prometheus shows high correlation with human evaluation and GPT-4 evaluation in absolute scoring settings, and also high accuracy in ranking scoring settings.

Despite these limitations, proprietary LLMs such as GPT-4 are able to evaluate scores based on customized score rubrics. Current resources, in contrast, are confined to generic, single-dimensional evaluation metrics that are either too domain/task-specific (e.g. EM, Rouge) or coarse-grained (e.g. helpfulness/harmlessness [11,19,13]), as shown in the left side of Figure 1. For instance, AlpacaFarm's [11] prompt gives a single definition of preference, asking the model to choose the model response that is generally preferred. However, response preferences vary based on specific applications and values. In real-world scenarios, users may be interested in a customized rubric such as “Which LLM generates responses that are playful and humorous” or “Which LLM answers with particularly care for cultural sensitivities?” Yet in our initial experiments, we observe that even the largest open-source LLM (70B) is insufficient to evaluate based on a customized score rubric compared to proprietary LLMs.

To this end, we propose Prometheus, a 13B LM that aims to induce the fine-grained evaluation capability of GPT-4 while being open-source, reproducible, and inexpensive. We first create the Feedback Collection, a new dataset crafted to encapsulate diverse and fine-grained user assessment score rubrics that represent realistic user demands (example shown in Figure 2). We design the Feedback Collection with these considerations in mind, encompassing thousands of unique preference criteria encoded by a user-injected score rubric. Unlike prior feedback datasets [20,21], it uses custom rather than generic preference score rubrics, to train models to flexibly generalize to practical and diverse evaluation preferences. Also, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to explore the importance of including various reference materials – particularly the ‘Reference Answers’ – to effectively induce fine-grained evaluation capability.

We use the Feedback Collection to fine-tune Llama-2-Chat-13B in creating Prometheus. On 45 customized score rubrics sampled across three test sets (MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, Feedback Bench), Prometheus obtains a Pearson correlation of 0.897 with human evaluators, which is similar to GPT-4 (0.882) and well above GPT-3.5-Turbo (0.392). Unexpectedly, when human evaluators were asked to choose the feedback of better quality in a pairwise setting, Prometheus was preferred over GPT-4 58.67% of the time, and it greatly outperformed GPT-3.5-Turbo with a 79.57% win rate. Also, when measuring the Pearson correlation with GPT-4 evaluation across 1222 customized score rubrics across 4 test sets (MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, Feedback Bench, Flask Eval), Prometheus showed higher correlation than GPT-3.5-Turbo and Llama-2-Chat 70B. Lastly, when tested on 2 unseen human preference datasets (MT Bench Human Judgments, HHH Alignment), Prometheus outperforms two state-of-the-art reward models and GPT-3.5-Turbo, highlighting its potential as a universal reward model.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- • We introduce the Feedback Collection dataset, specifically designed to train an evaluator LM. Compared to previous feedback datasets, it includes customized scoring rubrics and reference answers in addition to the instructions, responses, and feedback.

- • We train Prometheus, the first open-source LLM specialized for fine-grained evaluation that can generalize to diverse, real-world scoring rubrics beyond a single-dimensional preference such as helpfulness and harmlessness.

- • We conduct extensive experiments showing that by appending reference materials (reference answers, fine-grained score rubrics) and fine-tuning on feedback, we can induce evaluation capability into language models. Prometheus shows high correlation with human evaluation and GPT-4 evaluation in absolute scoring settings, and also shows high accuracy in ranking scoring settings.
